sections.title: Identifying data
notes: This is a FICTIONAL teaching case created for the demo. Juan is not a real person.
Juan, 28-year-old single man, call-center agent, first psychiatric admission.
Brought in by his older sister; informants: patient (fair reliability) and sister (good reliability).

sections.title: Chief complaint
notes: Sister: "He has not slept for a week and says the neighbors are recording him."
Patient: "I just need them to stop listening to my thoughts."

sections.title: History of present illness
notes: About 4 months PTA: social withdrawal after night-shift schedule change; stopped calling friends.
About 6 weeks PTA: started believing coworkers were reading his messages; locked his phone in a drawer.
About 2 weeks PTA: heard two male voices commenting on his actions, worse at night.
1 week PTA: decreased sleep (2–3 hours), poor intake, stopped going to work.
Day of admission: barricaded his room door; sister brought him to the ER.
Pertinent negatives: no mood elevation, no head trauma, no seizures, denies substance use (UDS pending at the time).

sections.title: Past psychiatric history
notes: No previous consults or admissions.
No prior self-harm; denies current suicidal or homicidal ideation (reassessed daily).
Occasional alcohol on weekends; no other substances by history.

sections.title: Medical, family and personal history
notes: Medical: unremarkable; no maintenance medications.
Family: paternal uncle 'had a nervous breakdown' in his 20s, details unknown.
Personal: college graduate, described as quiet but sociable; good premorbid functioning.

sections.title: Mental status examination
notes: Appearance: thin, unkempt, guarded, glances at the ceiling vent.
Speech: low volume, latency of response; thought process mostly goal-directed with occasional tangentiality.
Thought content: persecutory delusions, thought broadcasting.
Perception: second-person and third-person auditory hallucinations.
Mood "scared"; affect constricted, congruent. Oriented ×3. Insight: impaired (grade 2). Judgment: impaired.

sections.title: Laboratory and workup
notes: CBC, electrolytes, glucose, creatinine, TSH all within normal limits.
Urine drug screen negative; HIV and syphilis screen nonreactive.
Cranial CT: no acute findings. Baseline ECG: QTc 412 ms.

sections.title: Diagnostic formulation
notes: Working diagnosis: schizophreniform disorder (symptoms > 1 month, < 6 months), provisional.
Biological: possible family loading; sleep deprivation as precipitant.
Psychological: high stress, limited coping, social withdrawal.
Social: night shift, living alone, recent loss of peer contact.

sections.title: Management and course
notes: Started risperidone 1 mg at night, titrated to 3 mg/day by day 5.
Sleep normalized by day 4; voices less frequent by day 10.
Psychoeducation with sister; discharge on day 14 with weekly follow-up.

sections.title: Discussion and learning points
notes: Duration criteria separate brief psychotic disorder, schizophreniform disorder and schizophrenia.
Rule out medical and substance causes before labeling a primary psychotic disorder.
Shorter duration of untreated psychosis is linked to better outcomes.

qa.q: Why schizophreniform disorder and not schizophrenia?
a: Total duration of illness, including prodrome, is about 4 months.
Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least 6 months.
Labeled provisional because recovery is not yet established.
qa.tip: Lead with the duration criterion, then mention the provisional specifier.
qa.ref: DSM-5-TR, Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders

a: Brief psychotic disorder lasts at least 1 day but less than 1 month.
Juan's psychotic symptoms have been present for more than 1 month.

qa.q: What medical causes of psychosis did you rule out, and how?
a: Thyroid disease: normal TSH.
Infection: HIV and syphilis screens nonreactive.
Structural lesion: cranial CT without acute findings.
Metabolic: normal electrolytes and glucose.
qa.tip: Group them by system so it sounds organized.

qa.q: How did you exclude a mood disorder with psychotic features?
a: No sustained elevated or depressed mood episode by history.
Psychotic symptoms occurred without a concurrent major mood episode.
Urine drug screen negative.
Only occasional weekend alcohol; no withdrawal signs.
Symptoms persisted well beyond any plausible intoxication period.

qa.q: Why risperidone as the first-line agent?
a: Effective for positive symptoms in first-episode psychosis.
Available locally and affordable; long-acting injectable option exists later.
Start low, go slow in antipsychotic-naive patients.
qa.tip: Mention patient factors and availability, not just efficacy.

qa.q: What side effects do you monitor on risperidone?
a: Extrapyramidal symptoms and akathisia.
Hyperprolactinemia: sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia.
Metabolic: weight, waist, fasting glucose and lipids.
QTc at baseline and if dose increases.

qa.q: How long would you continue the antipsychotic after remission?
a: Common practice after a first episode: at least 1 to 2 years.
Decide jointly with patient and family; taper slowly if discontinued.

qa.q: What were the precipitating and perpetuating factors?
a: Precipitating: night-shift change and sleep deprivation.
Perpetuating: social isolation, impaired insight, living alone.
Supportive sister, good premorbid functioning, college education.
Acute onset and short duration of untreated psychosis.

qa.q: Was the admission voluntary? How was capacity assessed?
a: Fictional demo answer: admitted with patient's assent and family consent.
Capacity assessed on understanding, appreciation, reasoning and expressing a choice.
qa.tip: Know your hospital's actual admission policy for the real case.

qa.q: How do you handle confidentiality when the sister calls for updates?
a: Obtain the patient's consent on what may be shared.
Share general information needed for safety and aftercare planning.
